source.title_on_document: Sketching vs. AI Prompt Based Design Intent Evolution in Undergraduate Students: an Exploratory Study

supplement.where: The paper refers to no supplementary material or online appendix and gives no public data or code location. The PDF ends with references and contains no appendix (pp. 1-14).

paper_design_summary: The design-task analysis covered 61 eighth-semester industrial design students in a creative workshop offered within a mandatory course (p. 3, Section 3.1; p. 4, Section 3.2.3). Four student groups were randomly assigned to pen-and-paper sketching without devices (two groups, 31 students) or free use of LLM and text-to-image tools (two groups, 30 students); students worked individually for one hour on conscious water use at home (p. 4, Section 3.2.2). Three design professors rated the 115 included image-level ideas for creativity with CAT, and the authors counted ideas and categories and examined repeated concepts across students (pp. 4-5, Section 3.2.3; pp. 6-8, Sections 4.2.1-4.2.3).

studies.label: Design task: sketching vs generative AI (water-saving concept design)

assignment.what_was_assigned: The assignment unit was a student group: four groups were randomly assigned, two to sketching with pen and paper and no devices (A and C), and two to free use of generative AI tools (B and D). Students completed the task individually. The paper does not say how the groups were formed, whether they were classes or existing course sections, or how randomization was performed.
assignment.quote: the design task was carried out with four student groups, randomly assigned to two predefined conditions: sketch groups A+C (n=31) and AI groups B+D (n=30).

arms.name: Sketch groups (A+C)
arms.description: Pen and paper, no devices, and no other stimuli such as search engines or magazines. The paper calls these the control groups.

arms.name: AI groups (B+D)
arms.description: Own laptops or smartphones, with free use of any available LLMs (ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Copilot, etc.) and text-to-image tools (Krea.AI, Leonardo.AI, etc.). No prompting training. The paper calls these the experimental groups.

participants.exclusions: The design-task analysis is reported for 61 people (31 sketch, 30 AI), matching the counts given at assignment; no participant exclusions from the design task are stated (p. 4, Sections 3.2.2-3.2.3; p. 7, Section 4.2.3). The paper does not explicitly say whether every student contributed at least one rated image-level idea. Only ideas developed at image level with explanatory descriptions were rated; overly abstract AI images discarded by students were excluded, and image variations of one idea counted as one concept (p. 4, Section 3.2.3). The baseline AUT range counts are 25 high, 36 middle, and 7 low, summing to 68 rather than the stated 61 participants; the paper does not explain this discrepancy or specify when randomization occurred relative to the diagnostic phase, so no participant exclusions can be inferred from it (p. 5, Section 4.1; p. 3, Figure 1; p. 4, Section 3.2.2). Other analyses use subsets: 42 respondents to the optional diagnostic questionnaire (p. 5, Section 4.1), and 27 of the 30 AI conversation logs were analyzed after 3 incomplete or insufficient logs were discarded (p. 10, Section 4.2.6).
participants.who: Industrial design bachelor students in their 8th semester (4th of 5 years), 38 female and 23 male, ages 21 to 30 (mean 22), with mid-level design expertise. Design teachers recruited them by offering a creative workshop as part of their regular mandatory course.
participants.quote: A total of 71 ideas for the sketch group (n=31 students) and 44 ideas for the AI groups (n=30 students) were included in the PDF document.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2.3 (analyzed arm counts); p. 4, Section 3.2.2 (assignment); p. 3, Section 3.1 (population); p. 7, Section 4.2.3 (counts repeated)

ai_tool.name_model: Student choice, April 2025 (pp. 8-9, Section 4.2.5). LLMs: ChatGPT GPT-4o free with fallback (n=23), GPT-4o Plus (n=2), DeepSeek-R1 (n=3), Copilot (Azure-hosted GPT-4-class) (n=3), Gemini 2.5 (n=1). Text-to-image: Leonardo.AI Phoenix (n=15), Krea.AI Krea 1 (n=8), Meshy.AI (n=2), Vizcom (n=2), PromeAI (n=1), ArtGuru (n=1), GenCraft (n=1).
ai_tool.how_used: Free use of chatbots to explore the brief and generate ideas, and of text-to-image tools to render concepts. 28 of 30 AI students made their images from a prompt that the LLM wrote. Students got no prompting training, and some ran out of credits on image tools (pp. 4, 7, 9, 12-13).

task.description: Individual open-ended product design brief: 'how can we promote conscious water use in the home by its inhabitants?' Students were told to generate various ideas and detail a few. Sketch groups photographed their sketches. AI groups saved all conversations and images in a document.
task.duration: About 1.5 hours: 30 minutes for explanation and documentation and 1 hour for the creative exercise (p. 4).

outcomes.name: Expert-rated creativity of image-level ideas (CAT)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Consensual Assessment Technique on a 1-5 scale (1 = not creative, 5 = highly creative), three design professors with 10+ years of experience. Each idea is an image (sketch or AI image) with its explanatory text. AI image variations of one idea counted as one concept. The raters agreed on anchor examples, rated all 115 items alone, then re-rated them in reverse order. ICC (two-way random, consistency) = 0.67, 95% CI 0.55-0.76. Table 1 also gives medians and the share of ideas in four rating ranges. Rating procedures and ICC: pp. 4-5, Section 3.2.3.

contrasts.reported: Mean score per idea: sketch (A+C, n=71) 2.52 vs AI (B+D, n=44) 2.89. Median 2.67 vs 3.00. Low range (1-1.9) 18.3% vs 9.1%, medium (2.0-2.99) 52.1% vs 29.5%, medium-high (3-3.99) 26.8% vs 54.5%, high (4-5) 2.8% vs 6.8%. No SD, SE, or test for this comparison.

contrasts.treatment_arm: AI-labelled group printed as 'Group C (AI)', 24 ideas
contrasts.control_arm: Sketch-labelled group printed as 'Group A (Sketch)', 54 ideas
contrasts.reported: Group A (Sketch, n = 54, M = 2.36, SD = 0.61) vs. Group C (AI, n = 24, M = 2.94, SD = 0.58), t(76) = -3.995, p < .001, d = 0.60, 95% CI [-0.98, -0.47]. Independent-samples t-test with ideas as observations. Section 3.2.2 and Figure 1 put A and C both in the sketch condition, so the letters conflict. The printed d lies outside its printed interval (see open_questions).

contrasts.treatment_arm: AI-labelled group printed as 'Group D (AI)', 20 ideas
contrasts.control_arm: Sketch-labelled group printed as 'Group B (Sketch)', 17 ideas
contrasts.reported: Group B (Sketch, n = 17, M = 3.04, SD = 0.62) and Group D (AI, n = 20, M = 2.82, SD = 0.68), t(34.8) = 1.039, p = .306. Ideas as observations. Section 3.2.2 and Figure 1 put B and D both in the AI condition, so the letters conflict.

outcomes.name: Fluency: image-level ideas per participant
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of ideas developed at image level (sketches, or AI images with an explanatory description), counted by the researchers. These are the 115 ideas rated in S1-O1: 71 from 31 sketch students and 44 from 30 AI students.

contrasts.reported: 31 students generated 71 ideas based on sketches, and 30 students generated 44 ideas with AI on an image level. Average 2.2 ideas per participant with sketches vs 1.4 with images. Means only, no SD, SE, or test.

outcomes.name: Fluency: total ideas per participant (text and image)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of all ideas per participant at the total idea level: written ideas and sketches in the sketch groups, LLM-generated text ideas and text-to-image images in the AI groups. 89 ideas in the sketch groups and 291 in the AI groups. One AI participant had 41 ideas at the text level.

contrasts.reported: A total of 89 total ideas were generated by the sketch groups and 291 ideas for the AI groups. Mean 9.7 ideas per participant for AI and 2.8 for sketching. Means only, no SD, SE, or test.

outcomes.name: Flexibility: idea categories explored per student
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each participant's total ideas were listed in Excel and hand-sorted by the researchers into 12 categories (A raising awareness by measuring water use ... L gamification and educational challenges). The measure is the mean number of categories per student.

contrasts.reported: AI groups (B+D) present more categories than sketch groups (A+C), with an average of 4,2 versus 2 categories explored per student (decimal comma as printed). Means only, no SD, SE, or test.

outcomes.name: Homogenization of image-level concepts
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: The researchers inspected image-level concepts and counted the AI-group students whose concept was a shower or faucet with a red, yellow, and green light ring indicating water use (18 of 30 students, 60%; p. 6, Section 4.2.2). The observation for this proportion is a participant; the diversity construct concerns repetition of the concept across different participants. The sketch groups receive only a qualitative description, with no corresponding count (p. 7, Section 4.2.3).

contrasts.reported: Light-ring shower or faucet concept: 18 out of 30 students (60%) in the AI groups, and the pattern held regardless of AI model. Sketch groups: 'the images displayed more diversity depending on the type of solutions focused on local context' (no count). The direction is for diversity: lower in the AI arm.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section 4.2.2; p. 7, Figure 4 and Section 4.2.3

diversity_detail.metric: Share of AI-group students whose image-level concept was the same light-ring shower or faucet idea (18 of 30), otherwise a qualitative judgment
diversity_detail.computed_over: Image-level concepts of the 30 AI-group students, inspected by the researchers. Sketch-group images are described only qualitatively.
diversity_detail.notes: The paper reports homogenization, so the sign is reversed to diversity: the AI arm is lower. This is not a pairwise similarity measure. Its direction is opposite to S1-O6, which is measured at the total idea level.

outcomes.name: Category coverage of each condition's pooled total ideas
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Bubble charts of the number of total ideas per category (12 researcher-defined categories, A-L) for each condition's pooled ideas. Values read from Figure 5: sketch A16, B26, C2, D29, E6, F5, G3, H1, I1, with no ideas in J-L. AI A83, B39, C2, D59, E9, F4, G3, H5, I4, J30, K22, L31. The sums (89 and 291) match the printed totals. The two bubble charts represent two condition pools (sketch A+C and AI B+D), so n_units=2 counts sets, as identified in the Figure 5 caption (p. 8). The 380 constituent ideas are the corpus size, derived as 89 + 291, and are not the number of sets or independent observations.

contrasts.reported: Figure 5 caption: categories J, K, and L 'emerged in the AI group but were not explored by the sketch group.' Categories with at least one idea, counted from the figure: sketch 9, AI 12. The text does not print these counts.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Figure 5; p. 7, Section 4.2.3; p. 11, Section 5.1

diversity_detail.metric: Number of distinct researcher-defined categories covered by each condition's pooled total ideas, and ideas per category
diversity_detail.computed_over: All total-level ideas (text and image) of all participants in a condition, pooled
diversity_detail.notes: This is not a pairwise similarity measure. Coverage rises with the number of ideas, and the AI groups produced 291 ideas vs 89. The authors contrast this broader group-level design space with the homogenized image-level ideas (S1-O5).

company_involvement.description: None stated. Both authors are at UNAM's Industrial Design Research Center, the paper has no funding statement, and the acknowledgments thank lecturers and a student. Students used commercial AI tools of their own choice, and no company role is stated.

eligibility.reason: Four student groups were explicitly randomly assigned, two to sketching without devices and two to generative-AI access for their own creative work (p. 4, Section 3.2.2). Assignment is clustered; the groups are not identified as classes. The design-task analysis reports 61 people, 31 sketch and 30 AI, above the 50-person threshold (p. 4, Section 3.2.3; p. 7, Section 4.2.3). Three design professors rated produced images with explanatory text for creativity using CAT, with AI available to the AI arm while these outputs were created (p. 4, Sections 3.2.2-3.2.3). The unexplained baseline AUT counts totaling 68 do not override the explicit design-task counts (p. 5, Section 4.1). The unspecified randomization procedure, conflicting t-test group letters, inconsistent printed effect-size interval, and idea-level precision require extraction caveats, but do not unsettle these three criteria. Pooling requires uncertainty that accounts for the assigned groups and repeated outputs within people; the printed idea-level tests do not establish that precision (p. 6, Section 4.2.1; codebook Section 10).

one_line_finding: Expert creativity ratings of image-level ideas averaged 2.89 in the AI groups vs 2.52 in the sketch groups (44 vs 71 ideas, no test; Table 1, p. 6), but the two reported t-tests give mixed results (t(76) = -3.995, p < .001 and t(34.8) = 1.039, p = .306; p. 6), and AI students produced more total ideas (9.7 vs 2.8 per participant) but fewer image-level ideas (1.4 vs 2.2), with 18 of 30 converging on one light-ring concept (pp. 6-7).
open_questions: Group letters and pairing: Figure 1 and Section 3.2.2 assign A+C to sketching and B+D to AI (pp. 3-4), whereas the t-tests label A and B Sketch and C and D AI (p. 6, Section 4.2.1). Counts under the printed condition labels sum to 71 sketch and 44 AI ideas, matching Table 1, but the paper does not settle the correct group identities or why these pairs were tested. Author clarification is needed for extracting group contrasts; condition-level eligibility is unaffected.

Printed standardized effect: d = 0.60 lies outside the printed 95% CI [-0.98, -0.47] (p. 6, Section 4.2.1). The source gives no corrected value or explanation. The numbers remain recorded as printed, and their intended meaning requires author clarification; no alternative effect size has been computed.

Cluster assignment and precision: explicit random assignment of four student groups supports criterion 1, and the codebook permits clustered assignment (p. 4, Section 3.2.2; codebook Section 10). How the groups were formed and randomized is unstated. The printed creativity tests use ideas as observations; participant-level creativity summaries and precision accounting for the assigned groups are not reported (p. 6, Section 4.2.1). Author methods and data would be needed for valid pooled inference.

Design class: retain lab_rct for the supervised workshop exercise with a printed brief and fixed duration (p. 4, Section 3.2.2). Recruitment through a mandatory course makes field_rct an alternative interpretation (p. 3, Section 3.1), but this coding judgment does not change any eligibility criterion and needs no further source for screening.

Across-people primary record: total-idea category coverage is broader with AI (S1-O6), while image concepts show homogenization (S1-O5) (pp. 6-8, Sections 4.2.2-4.2.3; p. 11, Section 5.1). The paper names no primary outcome and neither measure is the semantic-similarity measure prioritized by codebook Section 8. Retain both with primary=not_stated; any selection for pooling requires an Atlas methods decision rather than an assumption about the paper.

Baseline AUT count discrepancy: 25 + 36 + 7 = 68 in the AUT score ranges, but the participant description and design-task assignment and analysis report 61 people (p. 5, Section 4.1; pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1 and 3.2.2-3.2.3). The paper does not explain the discrepancy or the timing of randomization relative to diagnosis. Authors would need to clarify it; the explicit design-task counts still meet criterion 2.

Recruitment location: the paper does not explicitly name the students’ university or workshop country. UNAM and Mexico City appear in author affiliations (p. 1); Mexico City dwellings appear as context for students’ ideas (p. 6, Section 4.2.1), not as an explicit recruitment location. Country is null pending author confirmation; this does not affect eligibility.
notes: Analyses not coded as outcomes: within-arm Pearson correlations of baseline AUT scores with design-task fluency (sketch r=.12, p=.54; AI r=.08, p=.67) and creativity (sketch r=.12, p=.53; AI r=-.30, p=.103) (p. 7, Section 4.2.4), which are not AI vs no-AI contrasts. The baseline AUT (Top2 scoring, Cronbach's alpha = 0.65, M = 2.8, SD = 0.51) is a pre-task measure, and its range groups sum to 25 + 36 + 7 = 68, not 61 (p. 5). Also not coded: the self-reported diagnostic and exit questionnaires (pp. 5, 10-11), the design paths (sketch 8 + 10 + 13 = 31, AI 22 + 7 + 3 = 32 for 30 students; p. 8), and the initial prompt strategies (13 + 7 + 6 = 26 for 27 analyzed logs; p. 10). The printed per-participant means equal the printed totals divided by the arm sizes, cut rather than rounded to one decimal (71/31 printed 2.2, 44/30 printed 1.4, 89/31 printed 2.8, 291/30 printed 9.7). Limitations the authors list: the sketch groups had no other stimuli such as search engines or magazines, the AI students had no prompting training and ran out of credits on some tools, and some students' ChatGPT had been 'trained' by earlier exercises (pp. 12-13). Recruitment site and country are not explicitly reported: UNAM and Mexico City are author affiliations (p. 1), and the reference to Mexico City dwellings concerns the context of students’ ideas (p. 6, Section 4.2.1). The form therefore does not assign the students to UNAM or infer a country. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as requested; the final decisions supersede its earlier assignment-unit coding.

differences.resolved: lab_rct, as in A. The design task was a one-off supervised session of about 1.5 hours with a printed brief written by the researchers, and the sketch groups were barred from devices. The paper presents it as a creative workshop offered within a mandatory course, never as coursework or a field experiment. The codebook defines lab_rct as a randomized experiment in a supervised session and field_rct as one inside the participants' ordinary work or coursework. Reconciled form c101 codes a one-protocol session held within a course as lab_rct, and c075 used field_rct only because that paper called itself a field experiment in an actual class. field_rct stays in open_questions as a possible reading.

open_items.item: Conflicting t-test group letters and unexplained pairing (original open question 1; p. 6, Section 4.2.1 versus pp. 3-4, Figure 1 and Section 3.2.2). Authors must identify the correct groups and paired comparisons. The explicit assignment and condition-level totals still support eligibility.

The printed d = 0.60 and 95% CI [-0.98, -0.47] are incompatible (original open question 2; p. 6, Section 4.2.1). An author correction is needed to identify the intended standardized effect and interval; no explanation is confirmed by the PDF. This affects effect extraction, not eligibility.

Whether group randomization qualifies (eligibility part of original open question 3): settled for screening by explicit random assignment of student groups (p. 4, Section 3.2.2) and the codebook’s provision for clustered assignment (Section 10). Criterion 1 is met; no unresolved eligibility question remains.

Formation of the four student groups and the randomization procedure are not described (methods part of original open question 3; p. 4, Section 3.2.2). Author methods would clarify these reporting gaps; the paper’s explicit statement of random assignment is sufficient for criterion 1.

Precision accounting for assigned groups and multiple ideas per student is unavailable (pooling part of original open question 3; p. 6, Section 4.2.1). Authors would need to provide ratings linked to participant and assigned group, with appropriate analysis, to establish uncertainty for pooling. This does not change the three screening criteria (codebook Section 10).

lab_rct versus field_rct (original open question 4 and resolved reconciliation difference): retain lab_rct for the supervised workshop protocol with a printed brief and fixed duration (pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1 and 3.2.2). The course setting permits an alternative label, but either randomized design class meets the same eligibility criteria; nothing further is needed for screening.

Across-people primary selection (original open question 5): the paper names no primary and reports category coverage and concept repetition at different output levels (pp. 6-8; p. 11, Section 5.1). Retain both with primary=not_stated. An Atlas methods decision would be needed for selecting between them; no missing source is needed to determine eligibility, already established by expert creativity ratings.

Baseline AUT ranges sum to 68 rather than 61, with no explanation or stated randomization timing relative to diagnosis (p. 5, Section 4.1). Authors must reconcile the counts and participant flow. Criterion 2 remains met by the explicit 31 sketch and 30 AI people analyzed in the design task (p. 4, Section 3.2.3; p. 7, Section 4.2.3).

Participant university and workshop country are not explicitly stated (p. 3, Section 3.1); author affiliations (p. 1) and a Mexico City example (p. 6, Section 4.2.1) do not establish recruitment location. Country remains null pending author confirmation. Location is not an eligibility criterion.
